messages.subject: Marker button & g.part4 error regarding sleeplog
messages.subject_clean: Marker button & g.part4 error regarding sleeplog
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

first, thanks for the great work on the GGIR package! It's works quite easy for analysing .bin-files. I'm currently testing the script with only a few .bin-files.

My first question is regarding the marker button on the GeneActiv device. We asked participants to press the button when going to sleep and when getting out of bed in the morning.
Is or will there be a version of the GGIR package incoroporating this marker button?

Second, I'm struggling with part 4 of the g.shell.GGIR function, when using a sleeplog.
I'm getting the following error:

Error in match.names(clabs, names(xi)) :
  names do not match previous names
In addition: Warning messages:
1: In which(sleeplog$id == as.numeric(accid)) : NAs introduced by coercion
2: In which(sleeplog$id == as.numeric(accid)) : NAs introduced by coercion

I'm not sure which names are meant in this error.
I do get some output, but only for one night.

I tried running the script without using a sleeplog, and then I also get the error regarding the names.

In the attachment is the used sleeplog, as wel as my script.

Thanks in advance!

Regards,
Chantal

> El miércoles, 31 de agosto de 2016, 21:01:29 (UTC+2), Vincent van Hees escribió:
>
> Hi Jairo,
> Good questions! I have inserted my answers in your email below.
> Best, Vincent
>
> On 31 August 2016 at 16:48, Jairo Hidalgo Migueles
> <jairo.hidal...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > 1- About device placement:  I believe that all algorithms (e.g. autocalibration, non-wear time and sleep time detection,...) implemented in GGIR have been developed for non-dominant wrist data, haven't it? If so, Could I expect a well-functioning of autocalibration (implemented with g.calibrate) for hip data? I think that non-wear detection and sleep algorithms are specific for device placement and they are not supposed to work well in hip for instance, have they been proved with hip data?
>
> >>> Answer: None the calculations in GGIR is body location specific and I have tried to design GGIR in a way that it could work for any body location. You a correct though that most of the work to support GGIR is based on wrist data, by which it is possible that GGIR is better justified for wrist data than for other body locations. However, I have good hope for its generic use for the following reasons:
> - The auto-calibration algorithm relies on having sufficient
> calibration points around the sphere (as explained in the  2014
> paper). This may easier with wrist data than with hip data, but the
> good thing about function g.calibrate is that it also evaluates its
> own performance and will tell you whether the autocalibration was
> successful; see QC output in GGIR. My experience is that the algorithm
> works fine for hip data, but as I said you will always be able to
> verify this yourself if in doubt.
>
>

> I am not sure to be agree in here. If I have understood well your 2014 paper, auto-calibration algorithm uses the time with no supposed body movement in which the acceleration measured should be only the gravitational one (=1g). And it is provided a correction factor based on that assumption (I understand that auto-calibration algorithm can work in any body location since it works with no-movement time, independently the placement). Then, considering that hip placement experiments more time without movement than wrist in free-living conditions, shouldn't get more data to populate the sphere using hip data?

>
> - Non-wear detection is by its own definition not body location
> specific. The algorithm is based on the signal noise level over large
> time windows, by default 1 hour. Therefore, I see no reason to doubt
> the performance of the non-wear detection for studies with different
> sensor attachment locations because we make all kinds of tiny
> movements with our body parts, which will trigger the wear-detection
> as soon as there is more variance in the data than would be expected
> from sensor noise. If you are in doubt then just do some experiments
> on yourself to see how GGIR handles an inactive day in the office or
> an evening behind the television and then investigate whether the code
> detects all your inactivity correctly as monitor-wear time.
>
>

> So, I can expect no misclassification between sedentary time and non-wear time due to these tiny movements that we produce even in hip (for example). Definitely I will prove it. I assume that using activity counts this misclassification is more likely because of all the smoothing process applied to the signal (they consider sedentary equal to non-wear time, =0 counts/min). I think this is one of the major advantages of working with raw data. Do you think that it is possible to apply smaller windows for non-wear detection (15 min instead of 60 min) without get a misclassification between these variables? I will prove on my own but I would like to know if you have already tested it.

>
>
> - The sleep detection algorithm is essentially a description of the
> data, as in: did the accelerometer orientation change by more than A
> degrees over a time window of B minutes. In my opinion there is
> nothing body location specific about that. Only when the
> wrist-specific parameters (5 degrees and 5 minutes) which I evaluated
> in last year’s paper are entered then the sleep detection will become
> wrist specific. So, in other words: A new set of parameters may make
> the algorithm equally well suitable for any other body location. All
> you need is a dataset to demonstrate that your new parameters are
> plausible for your new sensor location.
>
>

> Totally agree, thank you for the explanation. Maybe in hip placement the sleeplogs should be compulsory to use since sedentary people can register similar angle patterns in their hips during wake time.

>
>
> 2- MVPA cut-points: I've seen that MVPA time detection is done through
> cut-points based on different metrics (most of them on ENMO). I think
> this method is similar to the one applied with counts, and then it can
> have the same limitations. What is your opinion about that? Do you
> trust in cut-point methods to detect MVPA or do you know other methods
> that have been tested?
>
> >>> Answer: I am aware of the limitations of cut-points. I do not think that there is a convincing alternative approach available. Cut-points are easy to replicate which is good for methodological consistency, and easy to evaluate and update even by non-technical users. The relationship between acceleration and human energy expenditure is complex. Within single activity types the relationship between acceleration and energy expenditure may seem fairly linear. However, the linear relationship has a different slope and y-intercept between activity types (see my 2009 publication in Obesity), and those differences between activity types are in turn also dependent on body weight and age of the person being measured. So, if we consider real life conditions with a variety of activity types and a variety of individuals then the relationship between acceleration and energy expenditure is highly non-linear. One of the key problems in dealing with this non-linearity is that a substantial part of the non-linearity is actually caused by the energy expenditure construct itself and not by the limitations of the accelerometer. For example, MET values for the activity type sitting differ hugely between lean and overweight individuals, while the entire PA research community assumes that MET values are constant per activity types across individuals of the same age. Especially, in the activity type sitting it is impossible to blame the accelerometer because the accelerometer shows zero movement across individuals. Therefore, I have always been surprised to see that there are people who try to estimate MET values in sedentary activity types. There is no form of machine learning that can address this problem because this is a matter of measurement construct and not a problem of classification. IN conclusion, I think it is best to stick with cut-points because they at least have some informative value: higher is more movement of the accelerometer. This may not always be directly related to energy expenditure of the person as a whole, which warrants careful interpretation of acceleration data as proxy for energy expenditure. My personal view would be to stop attempting to say anything about energy expenditure with accelerometer data and use acceleration itself as the ground truth for physical activity, e.g. cut-points thresholds informed by acceleration values across activity types rather than informed by acceleration values across energy expenditure levels.

>
> Very interesting reasoning. Regarding energy expenditure in sedentary activities, and in concordance with my question above on non-wear time, I agree with you in trying to estimate MET values through activity counts is an impossible task during strictly defined sedentary activities (no movement, no counts). But using raw accelerations, as you said before we always do tiny movements, then, wouldn't be easier to adress this question with raw data? Anyway, we would always have the variance inter-individuals as a major problem (even using biometric data in the models it would be very difficult to solve). However, I think that your opinion about using acceleration values themselves is the best option. We would need reference parameters in different populations to correctly understand the data, but I think that it is the best way to exploit the potential of accelerometers

>
>
> > 3- Sedentary time: Is there any function in GGIR especialized in detecting sedentary time??
>
> >>> Answer: Not yet, but for the time being you could use argument ilevels to derive time spent below a certain threshold as a crude estimate of total time in sedentary behaviour

>
> Thank you, I will use it.

>
> > 4- Sleep time: Could you explain how to enter a sleeplog manually? It have to be done file with the arguments sleeplog_onset and sleeplog_wake? or is ther any easier method? And another question, I have run g.part4 in my data without entering a sleeplog, however, in the data frame resulting from that function I have variables called "sleeplog_onset", "sleeplog_wake", etc. Where these values come from if I didn't enter any sleeplog?
>
> >>> Answer: See attached document as example

> Thank you for the document. Then, when I run the code without using a sleeplog like that, why did I obtain values such as "sleeplog_onset"? I did not report any sleeplog onset, then, where does this value come from?

>
> > Thanks again for your work!
> > Best regards,
> > Jairo Hidalgo Migueles
messages.body_snippet:
Great thanks Vincent.
It is very helpful to know your thoughts. Find some opinions and more questions below.
Best,
Jairo

messages.subject: How does chunksize affect to the data?
messages.subject_clean: How does chunksize affect to the data?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

My question is about chunksize argument. I thought that chunksize only affects to the size of the blocks to process the data. Then I thought that changing the chunksize, the output would be the same, the unique difference should be the time spent in process the data and the number of blocks processed. But I tried the function g.calibrate in the same file with chunksizes = 1; and = 0.2, respectively and I obtained different offset and scale coefficients. Why does it happen?

Any help is more than welcome!

Best,
Jairo

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] How does chunksize affect to the data?
messages.subject_clean: [GGIR] How does chunksize affect to the data?
messages.body_plain:
Argument chunksize defines how big the blocks of data are that are loaded. The function g.calibrate stops when a certain hours of data are loaded as specified by minloadcrit and when the calibration criteria are met as explained in the paper. However, g.calibrate can only stop after an integer number of X hour blocks as defined by chunksize. If chunksizes are large it can load much more data then what you specified in minloadcrit. Therefore, chunksize setting can influence how much data is used and the data usage could impacts on the resulting calibration correction coefficients. A higher minloadcrit will typically result in more data and therefore more robust coefficients. To avoid working with unreliable correction coefficients, always check the calibration error indicator post calibration. My guideline would be to not work with data with an calibration error post calibration of 0.01g or higher.

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Some questions about GGIR package
messages.body_plain:
Regarding the calibration: It is not only the amount of data on the sphere but also the spread around the sphere. With hip data you have a reasonable chance that the participant never stands on their head, which means that there are no non-movement data points on the side of the sphere that would be covered by such an accelerometer orientation. This is why wrist data is probably easier to calibrate than hip, chest or ankle data. However, you would have to empirically evaluate this as it may still work.

Regarding the non-wear detection: I cannot say anything about this because you are using Actigraph on the hip. I have limited experience with this kind of data. You would have to investigate that yourself. The longer the window the smaller the change that inactivity gets misclassified as non-wear time.

Sleep: I think sleeplogs or marker buttons are advisable for all sensor locations, so not only the hip.

Interpretation of sleep variable names related to sleeplog: In the absence of a sleeplog the variable names referring to sleeplog actually relate to the assumed time in bed periods, e.g. def.noc.sleep interval.

Vincent

messages.subject: GGIR sustainability
messages.body_plain:
Dear GGIR users,

I am receiving requests for help and additional package functionality
on a weekly basis. It is great to see that people are so excited about
the package, but my time is limited. The package is released under the
open source license agreement, which does not mean that I have an
obligation to help you or that if I help you my time is for free.

Therefore, the future of GGIR depends on the willingness of me or
other people to continue developing and maintaining GGIR. This does
not only relate to desired functional improvements with clear
scientific impacts, but also relates to general investment in the
software quality and sustainability: readability of the code to enable
future developers to make improvements, speed of the code,
implementation of a much needed code test environment, more efficient
storage of the milestone data, better documentation, and possibly
various other aspects. None of these enhancement activities will
result in a scientific publication but if these activities are not
done the code is at risk of becoming obsolete in the upcoming
decade(s). Any piece of scientific software has this problem.

Ideally, there needs to be a community of GGIR developers in which
anyone is replaceable, including myself. For most computer scientists
this type of work is boring because the focus is not on innovation but
on sustainability and quality control. So, the only way to realise all
this is if you as GGIR end-users and stakeholders make a direct
investment. For example:
- Add a budget for a scientific programmer in your next grant
application to review and improve the GGIR code.
- Add a budget for a research assistant/technician in your next grant
application to learn GGIR and then educate other GGIR users via
courses/workshops, and respond to help requests on this email list.
- When you appoint your next student to develop new analytical methods
encourage them to re-use my code where possible instead of
re-inventing the wheel and starting from scratch. It took me six years
to develop GGIR to what it is today and I am sure you could safe
yourself a lot of time if you did at least consider re-using some of
the code.
- Don’t keep the developments to yourself but share them on github and
communicate what you are doing on this e-mail list such that efforts
can be coordinated. A GitHub repo of the current version of GGIR is
here, https://github.com/ucl-cls/mcs-acc, which is hosted by UCL in
London.

If you feel that you still need my involvement, then please get in
touch and we could explore commercial consultancy options, although my
time is limited. Finally, I would like to encourage scientists based
in The Netherlands to apply for funding at my employer:
www.esciencecenter.nl <http://www.esciencecenter.nl>.

With kind regards,

Vincent van Hees
